newsitem.title: FRANCE: French, German finance officials begin EMU talks.
newsitem.headline: French, German finance officials begin EMU talks.

text.p: France and Germany's top finance officials went into talks on Wednesday at which they were expected to try to dispel doubts about whether the European single currency would be launched on time in January 1999.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters he would reaffirm his belief that Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would start on January 1, 1999.

"I will reaffirm my conviction that we will be there on January 1, 1999," he told reporters as he arrived in the central French town of Lyon for talks with German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and French and German central bank heads Jean-Claude Trichet and Hans Tietmeyer.
The meeting, part of a regular series between the finance ministers and central bankers of Europe's two biggest economies, takes place amid resurgent speculation about a delay to EMU.
This has been fuelled by worries that Germany may be unable to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year in line with Maastricht treaty requirements.

But Waigel told Reuters that Germany was in a position to keep its deficit below three percent of gross domestic product this year, the key year for deciding which countries qualify to join a single currency when it is first launched in 1999.
He also said that both Germany and France were in a good position to achieve 2.5 percent economic growth this year.
Many private economists believe Germany will overshoot the three percent target, as unemployment, at a postwar record, bites into tax revenues.
Although the Maastricht treaty allows some leeway on deficits and debt, the question is complicated by Italy's insistence that it join the single currency from the start.
Germany is believed to be very reluctant to allow Italy, Spain and Portugal into EMU when it is first launched, fearing this would undermine the credibility of the new currency.
But any overshooting by Bonn on the deficit criterion will make it harder to exclude other countries, like Italy, expected by private economists to fall short of the three percent target.
A finance ministry official said earlier this week the talks, due to end with a joint news conference at 1145 GMT, would cover the economic outlook and progress towards EMU.
French and German finance ministers and central bankers meet regularly to hammer out a common position on European issues.

The official also said the talks would touch on France's proposal for a stability council to oversee economic policies in the euro zone and look at international efforts towards reducing taxation anomalies which give some countries an unfair competitive advantage.
